extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics instructors, mathematics education researchers, and mathematics majors
extracted.subtask_description: Strategies and evaluative facets for reading and understanding undergraduate-level mathematical proofs (what students should do when reading proofs and what instructors/researchers should assess). Draws on qualitative and survey studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy #1: Understand the Theorem Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Both pairs of students would invest time in trying to understand the theorem statement prior to reading its proof. Participants sought to gain this understanding by rephrasing the theorem in their own words or by expressing the theorem in logical notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rephrase the theorem informally in your own words to see what is assumed and what must be shown; alternatively express the claim in first-order/logical notation to permit symbolic/algebraic reasoning. Examples in the paper show students reformulating a k-tuply perfect number statement and constructing ∃x∈R (x^4 = x+1). Benefits: clarifies the claim and suggests how a proof might be constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy #2: Try to Prove the Theorem Before Reading Its Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Before reading each proof, successful students tried to prove the theorem themselves and only read the proof when progress stalled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting a proof helps identify high-level goals and techniques, makes you a more active reader, exposes tricks/techniques you can reuse, and provides practice writing proofs. Example: attempting to bound terms in 4x^3−x^4+2sin x = 30 helped students see the structure of the given proof and its two independent sub-parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy #3: Consider the Proof Framework Being Used
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend explicitly to what claim (or sub-claim) is being proven, which proof technique is being employed (e.g., direct proof, proof by contradiction, contrapositive), and what can be assumed vs. what must be shown within that framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify P and Q when relevant, locate where sub-proofs begin and end, and determine the role of clauses like 'on the other hand' to see hidden structural shifts. Doing so makes subtle features (e.g., two sub-proofs using different methods) visible and aids comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy #4: Break the Proof into Parts or Sub-Proofs (Partitioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: For proofs that can be decomposed, partition the proof to see where one part ends and the next begins, and treat lemmas/sub-proofs as separate components of the overall argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partitioning helps focus on high-level structure and avoid getting mired in technical details immediately. Students sometimes skip the proof of a lemma at first to understand how the lemma is used in the main argument. Benefit: breaks complicated proofs into manageable chunks and clarifies overall flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy #5: Use Examples to Make Sense of Statements Within the Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: When confused by an inference, instantiate the step with a concrete example or numeric case to see why the step holds and what the general pattern is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples not merely to verify but to reveal why a claim follows (e.g., using n=24 to see how a product expansion corresponds to divisors). Distinguish between mere empirical verification and using an example to illuminate the general mechanism behind a deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy #6: Compare the Method in the Proof to One's Own Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect on how the method used in the proof compares to how you would have approached the problem, noting novelty, utility, and transfer potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying surprising or clever techniques helps learners add methods to their repertoire and recognize when certain approaches are necessary (e.g., analytic bounding for polynomial+trigonometric equations). Use comparison to extract methods to apply in other problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof comprehension facet: meaning of terms and statements (local)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing the meaning of the terms and statements within the proof, including the meaning of the claim being proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At a local level, comprehension requires precise understanding of notation and claims; this supports subsequent line-by-line justification and prevents misunderstanding the theorem itself (the paper cites students often fail to understand statement before reading proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof comprehension facet: justify how assertions follow (local)
rubrics_metrics.description: Being able to justify how new assertions in a proof follow from previous ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local understanding includes being able to explain the logical or mathematical steps that connect statements. The literature cited shows students often focus on calculations and neglect justification of inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof comprehension facet: identify proof framework (local)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying the proof framework being used (e.g., direct proof, proof by contradiction) and seeing how assumptions and conclusions fit within that framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizing the proof scheme clarifies what can be assumed and what must be derived; this ties directly to Strategy #3 and helps detect structural issues like hidden sub-proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof comprehension facet: provide a summary emphasizing high-level goals (holistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a concise summary of the proof that emphasizes its high-level goals and main ideas rather than every computational detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holistic summary allows transfer and recognition of the proof's purpose. Strategies such as attempting the proof first and partitioning support producing such summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof comprehension facet: apply the methods of the proof in other situations (holistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to apply the methods used in the proof to prove new theorems or solve other problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehension includes seeing the proof technique as reusable; comparing methods (Strategy #6) and attempting proofs first fosters this facet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof comprehension facet: break proof into main parts or sub-proofs (holistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Break the proof into its main parts or sub-proofs as part of a holistic understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partitioning (Strategy #4) is explicitly listed in the holistic facets and aids both comprehension and summary formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof comprehension facet: apply general proof methods to a specific example (holistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to apply the general ideas or methods of the proof to a specific example (e.g., use proof for a general statement to explain a concrete instance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using examples (Strategy #5) is linked to this facet: instantiate proof ideas in concrete cases to demonstrate understanding and to see how the general method operates in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make important facets visible in proof presentation (transparency / structured proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should, where pedagogically appropriate, be presented in formats that make facets of understanding visible (e.g., structured proofs that expose summary and motivation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper discusses Hemmi's notion of transparency: aspects of proofs can be visible or invisible to students. While alternative structured formats have mixed empirical support, making high-level ideas and motivations explicit (or teaching students strategies to uncover invisible aspects) is recommended as a pedagogical option. Note: the paper also cites mixed evidence on the effectiveness of alternative proof formats and emphasizes active student engagement with proofs.
